youtube.aciklama:
We decode the abbreviations you see most often in audiology reports: PTA, SRT, SDT, SDS, MCL, UCL and NR. We also learn how decibel labels are used in a report, and the Latin and Greek roots such as oto, audio and vestibulo.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; ASHA, Guidelines for Determining Threshold Level for Speech; Stach, Comprehensive Dictionary of Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: PTA, SRT, SDS, UCL and the roots of the terms
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the abbreviations you will meet most often in an audiology report, and what they mean.
We will also learn the Latin and Greek roots of audiology terms, so you can decode new terms easily.
An audiology report carries many test results in a small space, so it is full of abbreviations.
Most of these abbreviations come from English test names and are used the same way in the international literature.
So knowing them makes it easier to read both reports and scientific papers.
In the clinic, these abbreviations are usually read letter by letter.
The rule is simple: the first time you use an abbreviation in a report, also write it out in full.
Most audiology terms come from a few Latin and Greek roots; knowing these roots makes new terms easier to decode.
The root oto means ear in Greek; otoscope, otology and otitis come from this root.
The root audi, or audio, comes from the Latin verb audire, to hear; audiology, audiometer and audiogram belong to this family.
The word acoustic also comes from a Greek verb meaning to hear.
The root vestibulo comes from the Latin vestibulum, entrance hall, and refers to the balance part of the inner ear.
Cochlea means snail in Latin, and the root of the word tympanic means drum in Greek.
The root presby means old; this is why age-related hearing loss is called presbycusis.
Endings at the end of a word also complete its meaning.
The suffix metry means measuring: audiometry measures hearing, and tympanometry measures the middle ear.
The suffix gram refers to the record or graph of a measurement: audiogram and tympanogram carry this suffix.
The suffix scope refers to an instrument for looking; an otoscope is an instrument for looking into the ear.
The suffix itis means inflammation; otitis media is inflammation of the middle ear.
Otalgia means ear pain and otorrhea means ear discharge; you will often see them in case history notes.

maddeler.metin: _dB SL_: relative to the person's threshold

cumleler: Almost every number in a report comes with decibels, and the label next to the decibel matters as much as the number.
dB HL is hearing level; audiogram thresholds, the speech recognition threshold and the uncomfortable level are written on this scale.
dB SPL is the physical sound pressure level; it is used in calibration and in otoacoustic emission, or OAE, measurements.
dB SL is the level relative to the person's own threshold; a test given forty decibels above the SRT is given at forty dB SL.
We will cover these three scales and their calculations in later decibel lessons; for now, reading the report is enough.
A decibel value without its label gives the reader incomplete information.
PTA stands for pure tone average, and it is the most common abbreviation in a report.
The classic PTA is the average of the air conduction thresholds at five hundred, one thousand and two thousand hertz.
In this example, these thresholds are twenty, thirty and forty decibels; the average is thirty decibels HL.
The World Health Organization and many current sources add four thousand hertz and use a four-frequency average.
If we also add the sixty decibels at four thousand hertz, the average becomes thirty seven and a half decibels HL.
So the report must always state which frequencies were used to calculate the PTA.
The table on screen summarizes the abbreviations you will meet most often; the first row is the PTA we just saw.
SRT is the speech recognition threshold, and it is written in decibels HL.
SDT is the speech detection threshold, the lowest level at which the person detects the presence of speech.
SDS is the speech discrimination score, and it is given as a percentage.
MCL is the most comfortable level.
UCL is the uncomfortable loudness level; both levels are written in decibels HL.
NR means no response: no response was obtained even at the maximum output of the device.
The SRT is the lowest level at which the person can correctly repeat about half of the words presented.
In Türkiye, common SRT lists use three-syllable words, while English lists typically use two-syllable spondees.
In the SDT, the person is not expected to understand the word, only to detect that speech is present.
So the SDT is usually about five to ten decibels lower, that is, better, than the SRT.
The SDT is especially useful in young children who cannot repeat words, and when there is no shared language.
As we saw in earlier lessons, the SRT and the PTA usually agree within ten decibels of each other.
The SDS shows what percentage of one-syllable words the person repeats correctly.
The test is given at a level comfortably above threshold, often thirty to forty decibels above the SRT.
In this example, the SRT is thirty decibels HL; the SDS was tested at seventy decibels HL, and the result is eighty eight percent.
In the report, write not only the percentage but also the test level, the ear and the word list used.
Some sources call the same test the word recognition score.
We will look at how to interpret the score in detail in the speech audiometry lessons later.
The MCL is the level at which the person listens to speech most comfortably.
The UCL is the level at which sound starts to become uncomfortable.
In people with normal hearing, the UCL is usually around one hundred decibels HL.
The range between threshold and UCL is called the dynamic range.
In this example, the SRT is forty, the MCL seventy five and the UCL one hundred five decibels HL; the dynamic range is sixty five decibels.
As the dynamic range narrows, it gets harder to make sounds audible without discomfort; this matters in hearing aid fitting.
Besides pure tone and speech tests, you will see other abbreviations in a report.
OAE stands for otoacoustic emissions; they reflect the function of the outer hair cells in the inner ear.
ABR is the auditory brainstem response, an objective test of the auditory nerve and the brainstem pathways.
With tympanometry results, you may see the acoustic reflex threshold, or ART.
ENT stands for ear, nose and throat; it often appears in the report as a referral recommendation.

cumleler.yazi: Some reports use Latin abbreviations for the ears: AD means right ear, auris dextra, and AS means left ear, auris sinistra.
cumleler.ses: Some reports use Latin abbreviations for the ears: A D means right ear, auris dextra, and A S means left ear, auris sinistra.

cumleler: These abbreviations can be confused with the names of tympanogram types, so it is safer to write right and left in full.

sahneler.metin: Write the report as if someone who does not know you will read it: spell out abbreviations at first use, add the decibel label, test level and list.
cumleler: A useful tip for report writing: write the report as if someone in another clinic who has never met you will read it.
Spell out each abbreviation at first use, and put the HL, SPL or SL label next to every decibel value.
For speech tests, state the level, the ear and the word list used.
That way, when the same person is retested in another clinic, the results can be compared with confidence.

maddeler.metin: SRT and SDT dB HL, SDS _percent_

cumleler: Oto means ear, audio hearing, metry measuring, gram record; knowing the roots helps you decode new terms.
PTA is the pure tone average; the report should state which frequencies were used to calculate it.
The SRT and SDT are written in decibels HL, while the speech discrimination score, SDS, is written as a percentage.
The MCL is the most comfortable level and the UCL the uncomfortable level; threshold to UCL is the dynamic range.

secenekler: Level for repeating half the words
sahneler.aciklama: The SRT is the lowest level at which _about half_ of the words are repeated correctly.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: what does the SRT, the speech recognition threshold, show?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: the lowest level at which about half of the words are repeated correctly.
The measure given as a percentage is the speech discrimination score, or SDS.
